questions.stem: A 58 year old man has a 14 month history of hesitancy, an intermittent stream and post-micturition dribbling. He gets up twice a night to pass urine. He has no weight loss or bone pain. Digital rectal examination shows a smooth, symmetrically enlarged, firm prostate with a preserved central sulcus. Urine dipstick is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Slowly progressive voiding LUTS and nocturia in a man over 50 with a smooth, firm, enlarged prostate is BPH.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: hesitancy, an intermittent stream and post-micturition dribbling
steps.x: Voiding symptoms plus a smooth, symmetrical, firm prostate in a man over 50.

elim: Usually painless visible haematuria, not slowly progressive voiding symptoms with a smooth enlarged gland.
Causes urgency and frequency, not hesitancy, an intermittent stream and an enlarged prostate.
Gives a hard, irregular, asymmetric gland with loss of the sulcus; this gland is smooth and symmetrical.
Causes a weak stream, but the prostate would not be enlarged and there is usually a history of trauma or STI.

steps.x: A. Benign prostatic hyperplasia. Smooth enlarged firm prostate + LUTS over 50 = BPH.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has a 3 year history of a weak stream, hesitancy and nocturia. His PSA is 2.9 µg/L (<4). Digital rectal examination shows a smooth, enlarged prostate. An MRI of the pelvis for an unrelated reason shows nodular enlargement of the gland immediately surrounding the proximal urethra.
questions.q: Which zone of the prostate is most likely to be affected?
questions.e: BPH arises in the transition zone around the proximal urethra, which is why it compresses the urethra and causes LUTS; cancer arises in the peripheral zone.

steps.x: The question asks: Which zone of the prostate is most likely to be affected? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Benign enlargement around the proximal urethra causing obstructive symptoms.

elim: This is non-glandular tissue and is not where BPH nodules arise.
Surrounds the ejaculatory ducts and is rarely the site of BPH.
The usual site of prostate cancer, not BPH.
Not part of the prostate and not a site of hyperplasia.

steps.x: E. Transition zone. BPH = transition zone; prostate cancer = peripheral zone.

questions.stem: An 82 year old man is seen at home by his GP for leaking urine day and night. He has had a poor stream for many years. He has no pain. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 142/84 mmHg. His abdomen is shown (see item resources).

visual.title: Where the mass is
visual.caption: A smooth, dull mass rising out of the pelvis: the chronically distended bladder.

questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on abdominal palpation?
o: Hard, irregular mass in the left iliac fossa
Pulsatile, expansile mass above the umbilicus
questions.e: Long-standing BPH causes chronic urinary retention: a firm, smooth, painless suprapubic mass with the rest of the abdomen soft and non-tender, often with overflow leakage.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on abdominal palpation? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Overflow leakage, years of weak stream, painless: chronic retention.

elim: Suggests a colonic tumour, not an obstructed bladder.
Describes an abdominal aortic aneurysm.
A tender bladder suggests acute retention; his retention is long-standing and painless.
Suggests appendicitis, not bladder outlet obstruction.

steps.x: A. Firm, smooth, painless suprapubic mass. Chronic retention = painless, smooth, firm suprapubic mass; acute retention is tender.

questions.stem: A 77 year old man with a long history of a weak urinary stream is on the orthopaedic ward 2 days after a hip replacement. He was nauseated overnight and given cyclizine. He has not passed urine for 10 hours and has severe lower abdominal pain. His pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 156/90 mmHg. There is a tender, dull suprapubic mass.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Pain, inability to void and a tender, distended bladder in a man with BPH, precipitated by cyclizine, is acute urinary retention.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
A known poor stream, an anticholinergic antiemetic, then painful anuria with a palpable bladder.

elim: Oliguria from AKI would not produce a tender, distended palpable bladder.
Chronic retention is painless; he has severe pain and a tender bladder.
Causes distension and vomiting, not a tender dull suprapubic mass and anuria.
Causes dysuria and frequency, not complete inability to void with a tender bladder.

steps.x: B. Acute urinary retention. Pain + cannot void + tender bladder = acute urinary retention; think cyclizine.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man has his third urinary tract infection in 9 months. He has had hesitancy and a weak stream for 6 years but has never sought treatment. His temperature is 37.4°C. Digital rectal examination shows a smooth, enlarged prostate. A bladder scan after voiding shows 380 mL of residual urine.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his recurrent infections?
questions.e: Bladder outlet obstruction from BPH leaves residual urine, and stagnant urine allows recurrent UTIs, bladder stones and hydronephrosis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of his recurrent infections? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: third urinary tract infection in 9 months
steps.x: Recurrent UTI plus a large residual volume behind an enlarged prostate.

elim: Would cause pneumaturia or faecaluria, which he does not have.
Can predispose to infection but does not explain the large post-void residual.
The gland is smooth; cancer does not explain repeated infection better than stasis.
Would not cause an enlarged prostate; his obstruction is prostatic.

steps.x: C. Incomplete bladder emptying. Residual urine from BPH obstruction = recurrent UTI.

questions.stem: A 79 year old man has had a weak stream and nocturia for 8 years. He is now tired and has lost his appetite. A smooth, painless suprapubic mass is palpable. His BP is 152/88 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on renal tract ultrasound?
o: Single calculus in the right ureter
questions.e: Chronic bladder outlet obstruction from BPH raises bladder pressure, which is transmitted up both ureters, causing bilateral hydronephrosis and renal impairment.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on renal tract ultrasound? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: weak stream and nocturia for 8 years
tired and has lost his appetite
steps.x: Chronic retention and a rising creatinine: obstruction below both kidneys.

elim: Suggests chronic pyelonephritis or long-standing CKD, not acute back-pressure from outlet obstruction.
Suggests polycystic kidney disease.
Would cause unilateral, painful obstruction, not bilateral painless back-pressure.
Suggests renal cell carcinoma; it would not explain bilateral obstruction.

steps.x: A. Bilateral hydronephrosis. Outlet obstruction affects both kidneys = bilateral hydronephrosis.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man has had nocturia, a weak stream and hesitancy for 3 years. He is otherwise well with no weight loss or bone pain. Digital rectal examination shows a smooth, symmetrical, firm, enlarged prostate estimated at 50 g with a preserved central sulcus.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A mildly raised PSA fits BPH, because a bigger mass of glandular tissue makes more PSA; the smooth, symmetrical gland points away from cancer.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: no weight loss or bone pain
steps.x: A smooth large gland and a PSA only just above the cut-off.

elim: Causes fever, perineal pain and an exquisitely tender prostate.
There is no palpable bladder; this describes the underlying cause, not a complication.
Typically a hard, irregular, asymmetric gland and a markedly raised PSA.
Does not enlarge the prostate.

steps.x: B. Benign prostatic hyperplasia. BPH: PSA normal or only mildly raised.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man has a 1 year history of needing to rush to the toilet and passing urine every 2 hours. He also has to wait for his stream to start, it stops and starts, and he feels he has not emptied his bladder. Urine dipstick is negative. His prostate is smooth and enlarged.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
questions.e: BPH causes both storage (frequency, urgency) and voiding (hesitancy, intermittency, incomplete emptying) LUTS.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of his symptoms? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: wait for his stream to start
steps.x: Voiding symptoms plus an enlarged prostate, with storage symptoms as well.

elim: Explains urgency and frequency, but not hesitancy, an intermittent stream and incomplete emptying.
Causes large volumes and thirst, not voiding symptoms with an enlarged prostate.
Causes bladder pain and frequency, usually in women, with a normal prostate.
The dipstick is negative.

steps.x: A. Benign prostatic hyperplasia. Mixed storage and voiding LUTS with an enlarged prostate = BPH.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man comes to the emergency department at 2 am. He has not been able to pass urine since a wedding reception where he drank a lot of beer. He has had a weak stream for 2 years. He is distressed and in pain. His pulse rate is 108 bpm and BP 160/94 mmHg.

visual.title: Where the pain is
visual.caption: A tender, dull, distended bladder above the pubis.

questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of the abdomen?
o: Tender right iliac fossa with rebound
Tender, distended bladder palpable above the pubis
questions.e: Acute urinary retention on a background of BPH causes pain, inability to void and a distended, tender, palpable bladder; alcohol is a classic trigger.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on examination of the abdomen? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: not been able to pass urine
steps.x: Sudden painful inability to void after a large fluid and alcohol load, on a background of a poor stream.

elim: Suggests peritonitis, not a single obstructed organ.
Describes chronic retention, which is painless.
Suggests an aortic aneurysm.
Suggests appendicitis.

steps.x: E. Tender, distended bladder palpable above the pubis. Acute retention = painful, tender, distended bladder; treat with immediate catheterisation.

questions.stem: A 73 year old man is catheterised for acute urinary retention, which drains 1100 mL. He has had nocturia, hesitancy and a weak stream for 5 years. He has no weight loss, back pain or haematuria. Digital rectal examination shows a smooth, firm, enlarged prostate.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of his retention?
questions.e: Years of LUTS and a smooth enlarged prostate make BPH the cause; prostate cancer arises peripherally and does not typically cause acute retention.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely underlying cause of his retention? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: nocturia, hesitancy and a weak stream for 5 years
steps.x: A long history of obstructive symptoms and a smooth enlarged gland.

elim: Can block the outlet, but it would not explain years of LUTS with a smooth enlarged gland.
No history of constipation, and the DRE shows an enlarged prostate rather than faeces.
Does not typically present with acute retention, and the gland is smooth rather than hard and irregular.
Would not cause an enlarged prostate.

steps.x: A. Benign prostatic hyperplasia. Acute retention in an older man with years of LUTS = BPH until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: An 84 year old man has started wetting the bed at night for the past 2 months. During the day he passes small amounts often and dribbles afterwards. He has no pain or fever. His temperature is 36.6°C. There is a smooth, painless, dull mass arising from the pelvis. Urine dipstick is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his bedwetting?
questions.e: Chronic retention from BPH overfills the bladder until it overflows, often first noticed as night-time incontinence; the bladder is a painless suprapubic mass.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of his bedwetting? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: smooth, painless, dull mass arising from the pelvis
steps.x: Small frequent voids, nocturnal leakage and a painless palpable bladder.

elim: Causes urge incontinence with normal emptying, not a palpable painless bladder.
Produces large night-time volumes, not small frequent voids with a distended bladder.
Leakage with coughing, rare in men without prostate surgery.
The dipstick is negative and he has no fever or dysuria.

steps.x: C. Overflow from chronic urinary retention. Elderly man + new bedwetting + painless bladder = chronic retention with overflow.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man has had a poor stream for 10 years. He now strains to void and passes only small volumes. A bladder scan after voiding shows 520 mL. Renal function is normal. He has never had treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on ultrasound of the bladder wall?
o: Papillary mass on the bladder wall
questions.e: Long-standing outlet obstruction makes the detrusor hypertrophy (a thick, trabeculated wall) before it decompensates and fails to empty.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on ultrasound of the bladder wall? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
A decade of obstruction and now a large residual.

elim: Seen in schistosomiasis, not BPH.
Years of obstruction cause detrusor hypertrophy, so the wall would not be normal.
Suggests bladder cancer.
Suggests interstitial cystitis or tuberculosis; his bladder holds a large residual.

steps.x: E. Thickened, trabeculated bladder wall. Obstruction: detrusor hypertrophy first, then decompensation.

questions.stem: A 75 year old man with untreated BPH has suprapubic discomfort. His stream sometimes stops suddenly in the middle of voiding, and he notices blood at the end of passing urine. His temperature is 36.9°C. A plain X-ray shows a round opacity in the midline of the pelvis.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Stasis of residual urine in BPH leads to bladder stones, which roll over the outlet and stop the stream mid-flow, with terminal haematuria.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: stops suddenly in the middle of voiding
round opacity in the midline of the pelvis
steps.x: A stream that stops mid-flow, terminal haematuria and a midline pelvic opacity.

elim: Causes painless haematuria but not a sudden mid-stream stop with a midline opacity.
Small, round and lateral; it does not cause symptoms.
Causes fever, perineal pain and a tender prostate.
Causes colicky loin-to-groin pain, and lies lateral along the ureter.

steps.x: A. Bladder calculus. Residual urine in BPH predisposes to bladder stones.

questions.stem: A 64 year old keen cyclist has nocturia and a weak stream. Digital rectal examination shows a smooth, enlarged prostate. His GP plans to check his PSA. He rode 60 miles yesterday and had sexual intercourse last night. He has had no urinary infection.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice before PSA testing?
o: Avoid ejaculation and vigorous exercise for 48 hours
Fast for 12 hours before the test
questions.e: PSA testing needs counselling: avoid ejaculation and vigorous exercise for 48 hours beforehand, and wait 6 weeks after UTI, prostatitis or biopsy.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate advice before PSA testing? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Both recent cycling and ejaculation can raise PSA.

elim: Alcohol does not affect PSA.
PSA does not need a fasting sample.
Recent ejaculation and vigorous exercise can falsely raise PSA.
The 6 week wait is for recent UTI, prostatitis or biopsy, which he has not had.

steps.x: B. Avoid ejaculation and vigorous exercise for 48 hours. Ejaculation/exercise: wait 48 hours. UTI/prostatitis/biopsy: wait 6 weeks.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man has lower urinary tract symptoms. Ten days ago he finished antibiotics for acute bacterial prostatitis and he now feels well. Digital rectal examination today shows a smooth, enlarged, non-tender prostate. He asks to have his PSA checked today.
questions.q: When is the most appropriate time to measure his PSA?
questions.e: Prostatitis disrupts the gland and raises PSA, so testing waits 6 weeks after infection, prostatitis or biopsy.

steps.x: The question asks: When is the most appropriate time to measure his PSA? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Recent prostatic inflammation.

elim: 48 hours is the interval after ejaculation or exercise, not infection.
Longer than needed; 6 weeks is enough for PSA to settle.
PSA is part of assessing LUTS and should still be checked after the safe interval.
Recent prostatitis falsely raises PSA, so a result now would be misleading.

steps.x: C. 6 weeks after the prostatitis. After UTI, prostatitis or biopsy: wait 6 weeks for PSA.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has had a weak stream, hesitancy and nocturia for a year. He has no fever or dysuria. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 72 bpm and BP 136/80 mmHg. His abdomen is soft with no palpable bladder. Urine dipstick is negative for leucocytes and nitrites.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in his assessment?
o: CT of the abdomen and pelvis
questions.e: First-line assessment of LUTS is a urine dipstick to exclude infection and a DRE to feel for a smooth, enlarged, firm prostate.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next step in his assessment? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Infection has been excluded; now examine the prostate.

elim: Not a first-line test for LUTS.
Used for haematuria, not as a first assessment of LUTS.
Only after an abnormal MRI for suspected cancer.
Reserved for complex cases or before surgery, not first-line.

steps.x: C. Digital rectal examination. LUTS: dipstick, then DRE (plus counselled PSA).

questions.stem: A 63 year old man complains that his stream is weak and takes a long time. Urine dipstick is negative and digital rectal examination shows a smooth, enlarged prostate. The urology nurse wants an objective measure of how fast he passes urine.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Second-line tests for LUTS are uroflowmetry (a reduced maximum flow rate) and bladder ultrasound for post-void residual.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: objective measure of how fast he passes urine
steps.x: They want to quantify flow rate.

elim: Images the urinary tract for haematuria; it does not measure flow.
Looks inside the bladder but does not measure flow rate.
Used for suspected cancer, not for measuring flow.
Looks for malignant cells, not obstruction.

steps.x: E. Uroflowmetry. Flow rate = uroflowmetry; incomplete emptying = post-void bladder scan.

questions.stem: A 78 year old man has had a weak stream for years and now feels he never empties fully. He has had two UTIs this year. Dipstick today is negative. Digital rectal examination shows a smooth, enlarged prostate. His abdomen is soft and a bladder cannot be felt confidently because of his body habitus.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Ultrasound of the bladder after voiding measures the post-void residual, showing incomplete emptying and chronic retention.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
The question is how much urine is left behind.

elim: Will not measure residual volume.
Exposes him to radiation and is not needed to measure residual urine.
Does not measure residual volume and is invasive.
Already negative; it will not show whether he empties.

steps.x: D. Post-void bladder ultrasound. Incomplete emptying in BPH: post-void bladder ultrasound.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man has had nocturia twice nightly, a weak stream and some straining for 9 months. Dipstick is negative and his prostate is smooth and enlarged. The GP wants to grade how severe and bothersome his symptoms are before deciding on treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate tool to use?
questions.e: IPSS scores frequency, nocturia, urgency, weak stream, straining, incomplete emptying and quality of life; it guides whether treatment is conservative or drug-based.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate tool to use? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: grade how severe and bothersome his symptoms are
steps.x: A symptom severity score for LUTS.

elim: Grades prostate cancer on biopsy, not symptoms.
Measures consciousness.
Scores the likelihood of cancer on MRI, not symptom severity.
Estimates the probability of DVT or PE.

steps.x: C. International Prostate Symptom Score. LUTS severity = IPSS (≤7 mild, >7 moderate to severe).

questions.stem: A 57 year old man has mild nocturia and occasional hesitancy. He drinks five cups of coffee a day and two pints of beer most evenings. Urine dipstick is negative and his prostate is smooth and mildly enlarged. His IPSS is shown (see item resources).

visual.title: IPSS
visual.label: IPSS 5
visual.caption: A score of 7 or less is mild.

questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Reduce caffeine, alcohol and evening fluids
questions.e: Mild LUTS (IPSS 7 or less) is managed conservatively: cut caffeine and alcohol and reduce fluids before bed.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial management? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: five cups of coffee a day
two pints of beer most evenings
steps.x: Mild symptoms with obvious lifestyle triggers.

elim: For a large prostate or when an alpha-blocker cannot be used, not mild symptoms.
First-line drug only when IPSS is more than 7.
Added for persisting storage symptoms, not first-line.
Reserved for severe, refractory disease.

steps.x: B. Reduce caffeine, alcohol and evening fluids. IPSS ≤7: conservative; IPSS >7: alpha-blocker.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man with BPH has an IPSS of 16. His prostate is estimated at 25 g. He has no history of falls or dizziness. His GP starts tamsulosin and counsels him about side effects.
questions.q: Which side effect is he most likely to be warned about?
questions.e: Alpha-1 antagonists cause dizziness, postural hypotension, dry mouth and rhinitis, so they are avoided in men with falls or orthostatic hypotension.

steps.x: The question asks: Which side effect is he most likely to be warned about? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
An alpha-1 antagonist for moderate symptoms.

elim: A side effect of finasteride, not tamsulosin.
Not a recognised effect of alpha-blockers.
Typical of 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors.
Tamsulosin relieves obstruction; antimuscarinics and cyclizine can cause retention.

steps.x: C. Postural hypotension. Tamsulosin: dizziness and postural hypotension; finasteride: sexual side effects and gynaecomastia.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man has troublesome nocturia, straining and a weak stream. His IPSS is 22. Digital rectal examination shows a smooth, very large prostate and ultrasound estimates it at 75 g. His PSA is 3.6 µg/L (<4). He has no history of falls and his BP is 138/82 mmHg with no postural drop.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: A significantly enlarged prostate with severe symptoms is treated with combination therapy: an alpha-1 antagonist for quick relief plus a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor to shrink the gland.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Severe symptoms and a big gland in a man who can take an alpha-blocker.

elim: Treats nocturnal polyuria, not outlet obstruction from a large gland.
His IPSS is well above 7.
Relieves symptoms but will not shrink a gland this large.
An antimuscarinic alone could worsen voiding in severe obstruction.

steps.x: D. Tamsulosin and finasteride. Large prostate + bothersome LUTS = alpha-blocker plus 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man with a 55 g prostate starts finasteride. Four weeks later he returns, disappointed that his stream is no better. He has no new symptoms and his BP is 134/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Continue, as it takes about 6 months to work
Stop it, as it has failed
questions.e: Finasteride blocks DHT production and slowly shrinks the gland, so benefit takes around 6 months, unlike the rapid effect of tamsulosin.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate advice? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
A slow-acting drug judged too early.

elim: He has no persisting storage symptoms, and finasteride has not had time to work.
Finasteride is given at a fixed dose; the issue is time, not dose.
Surgery is for severe disease refractory to adequate medical treatment.
Four weeks is too soon to judge it.

steps.x: B. Continue, as it takes about 6 months to work. 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor: ~6 months to work; alpha-blocker: days to weeks.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man with BPH has taken tamsulosin for 4 months. His stream is now good and he no longer strains. However, he still has urgency and passes urine every hour during the day. Urine dipstick is negative. A post-void bladder scan shows 40 mL.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: If storage symptoms persist after an alpha-blocker and the residual is low, add an antimuscarinic such as tolterodine, darifenacin or oxybutynin.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Voiding fixed, storage symptoms persist, and he empties well.

elim: Shrinks the gland but does not target persisting urgency when voiding has already improved.
Reduces nocturnal urine production; his problem is daytime urgency.
It has helped his voiding symptoms.
Not indicated; his obstruction is controlled.

steps.x: B. Add tolterodine. Persisting mixed symptoms on tamsulosin: add an antimuscarinic.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man with BPH has taken tamsulosin and finasteride for 18 months. His IPSS remains 27, he has had two episodes of acute retention needing catheterisation and a bladder stone. His PSA is 1.9 µg/L (<4) and he is fit for surgery.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Severe disease refractory to medical therapy, with retention and stones, is treated with TURP.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Failed combination therapy plus complications.

elim: An antimuscarinic could worsen retention.
Maximal medical treatment has already failed.
Reserved for men unfit for surgery.
A cancer operation; this is benign disease.

steps.x: E. Transurethral resection of the prostate. Severe refractory BPH = TURP.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man has been unable to pass urine for 9 hours and is in severe lower abdominal pain. He has had a weak stream for 3 years. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 112 bpm and BP 168/96 mmHg. A tender suprapubic mass is palpable and a bladder scan shows 950 mL.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: Acute urinary retention is relieved immediately with a urinary catheter; drugs and surgery come later.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial management? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: unable to pass urine for 9 hours
steps.x: Painful, confirmed acute retention.

elim: Will add to the volume in an obstructed bladder.
May help a later trial without catheter but does not relieve retention now.
Not an emergency treatment for acute retention.
Delays relief; the diagnosis is already clear on the bladder scan.

steps.x: D. Urethral catheterisation. Acute urinary retention = catheterise now.

questions.stem: A 79 year old man with BPH started tamsulosin 3 weeks ago. Since then he has become light-headed when he stands and has fallen twice. His lying BP is 138/78 mmHg and standing BP 108/64 mmHg. His IPSS is 17 and his prostate is estimated at 45 g.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate change to his treatment?
questions.e: Alpha-1 antagonists are contraindicated with falls or orthostatic hypotension; a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor is used instead when the gland is over 30 g.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate change to his treatment? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Postural hypotension and falls on an alpha-blocker, with an enlarged gland.

elim: Another alpha-1 antagonist, with the same postural hypotension risk.
Does not address the falls, and does not treat obstruction.
Treats the side effect with another drug instead of removing the cause.
He still has moderate symptoms and a prostate over 30 g.

steps.x: E. Stop tamsulosin and start finasteride. Falls on tamsulosin: switch to finasteride.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man with BPH asks why his prostate is enlarging. His urologist explains that testosterone is converted within the prostate into a more potent hormone that drives cell growth, and that his new tablet blocks this conversion.
questions.q: Which hormone most directly drives prostatic growth?
questions.e: 5-alpha-reductase converts testosterone to DHT, which drives prostatic growth; finasteride shrinks the gland by blocking DHT production.

steps.x: The question asks: Which hormone most directly drives prostatic growth? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

clues: converted within the prostate into a more potent hormone
steps.x: The question wants the potent hormone made from testosterone.

elim: Acts on Sertoli cells in the testis, not directly on the prostate.
Not the main driver of BPH.
Not the driver of prostatic hyperplasia.
Is the precursor; 5-alpha-reductase converts it into the more potent DHT.

steps.x: A. Dihydrotestosterone. BPH is driven by DHT, made from testosterone by 5-alpha-reductase.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man takes tamsulosin for BPH. His stream improved within a week, but he has noticed dizziness on standing and a blocked nose. His prostate volume on ultrasound is unchanged after 6 months.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his side effects?
o: Blockade of alpha-1 receptors in vascular smooth muscle
Blockade of muscarinic receptors in the bladder
Stimulation of beta-3 receptors in the bladder
questions.e: Tamsulosin relaxes alpha-1-mediated smooth muscle in the prostate and bladder neck quickly but does not shrink the gland; blocking vascular and nasal alpha-1 receptors causes postural hypotension and rhinitis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of his side effects? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Fast effect, no shrinkage, vasodilatory side effects.

elim: The mechanism of tolterodine and oxybutynin.
The mechanism of finasteride, which causes sexual side effects, not dizziness.
Would shrink the gland, which has not happened.
The mechanism of mirabegron.

steps.x: A. Blockade of alpha-1 receptors in vascular smooth muscle. Alpha-1 blockade relaxes smooth muscle: quick relief, no shrinkage, postural hypotension.

questions.stem: A 73 year old man has a TURP for severe BPH. The prostate chips are sent for histology. He has no history of cancer and his PSA was 2.2 µg/L (<4). The pathologist reports that there is no malignancy.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on histology?
o: Atypical glands with prominent nucleoli invading stroma
Hyperplasia of glandular epithelium and fibromuscular stroma
questions.e: BPH is non-malignant proliferation of both glandular epithelium and fibromuscular stroma in the transition zone around the urethra.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on histology? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
Benign enlargement removed at TURP.

Suggest tuberculosis.
Suggests acute prostatitis.

steps.x: D. Hyperplasia of glandular epithelium and fibromuscular stroma. BPH = hyperplasia of epithelium and stroma, not malignancy.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man with lower urinary tract symptoms has a smooth, symmetrically enlarged prostate of about 70 g. His PSA is 5.4 µg/L (<4). MRI of the prostate shows diffuse transition zone enlargement and no focal lesion (PI-RADS 2).
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for his PSA level?
questions.e: More glandular tissue makes more PSA, so BPH can mildly raise PSA; this must be distinguished from the pattern in prostate cancer.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely explanation for his PSA level? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

steps.x: C. Increased mass of glandular tissue. BPH raises PSA mildly through glandular volume.

questions.stem: A 78 year old man with BPH is admitted with labyrinthitis and is given an antiemetic. Eight hours later he cannot pass urine and has a painful distended bladder. His other medicines have not changed.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism by which the antiemetic precipitated his retention?
o: Alpha-1 receptor blockade at the bladder neck
questions.e: Cyclizine is an antihistamine with antimuscarinic effects that weaken detrusor contraction, tipping an obstructed BPH bladder into acute retention.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism by which the antiemetic precipitated his retention? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.

steps.x: B. Antimuscarinic reduction of detrusor contraction. Cyclizine (anticholinergic) precipitates acute retention in BPH.

questions.stem: An 80 year old man has had a poor stream for 12 years. He has never been treated. His bladder holds 900 mL after voiding but he feels no discomfort. Two years ago an ultrasound showed a thick-walled bladder that emptied to 100 mL.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his large painless bladder?
questions.e: In chronic obstruction the detrusor first hypertrophies to push urine past the gland, then decompensates, leading to incomplete emptying, residual urine, infection and hydronephrosis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of his large painless bladder? Decide what kind of answer you need before reading the options.
A thick bladder that once emptied now holds a large painless residual.

elim: Would cause urgency and small volumes, not a large residual.
Would cause pain and frequency.
Prostate cancer does not typically cause early obstruction.
He has no neurological symptoms and the history is 12 years of obstruction.

steps.x: A. Detrusor decompensation after hypertrophy. Detrusor hypertrophy, then decompensation, then chronic retention.
